Algorithm: 1. Partition batch across GPUs 2. Each GPU computes the forward pass on its partition 3. Each GPU computes gradients via backpropagation 4. All-reduce operation averages gradients across GPUs 5. Each GPU updates its model parameters 6.6.2 Model Parallelism For models too large to fit on a single GPU, different layers or attention heads are placed on different GPUs. T ensor Parallelism: Splits individual tensors (e.g., weight matrices) across GPUs, requiring commu- nication during forward and backward passes. Pipeline Parallelism: Assigns different layers to different GPUs, processing micro-batches in a pipelined fashion to reduce idle time. Chapter 7 Conclusion and Future Directions This comprehensive treatment has established the mathematical foundations of attention mechanisms and their implementation in the Transformer architecture. From the fundamental attention operation through multi-head attention, positional encoding, and training dynamics, we have developed a rigorous understand- ing of these powerful sequence modeling tools. Attention mechanisms represent a fundamental paradigm shift in how neural networks process sequential information, moving from fixed compression through recur- rent states to flexible, learned aggregation patterns. The success of Transformers across natural language processing, computer vision, and multimodal domains demonstrates the broad applicability of this approach. 7.1 Achievements and Impact The Transformer architecture has fundamentally reshaped modern machine learning. Large language models built on Transformer foundations, including GPT-3 [5], PaLM [8], and LLaMA [30], have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across diverse tasks through in-context learning and few-shot adaptation. These models have achieved performance levels that approach or exceed human capabilities on many benchmarks, while also revealing emergent properties not present in smaller-scale systems. Beyond language processing, attention mechanisms have enabled breakthroughs in protein structure prediction through AlphaFold [20], revolutionized computer vision with Vision Transformers [12], and facilitated multimodal understanding through models like CLIP [24] and Flamingo [1]. The versatility of attention as a general-purpose mechanism for relationship modeling has proven applicable across scientific domains, from molecular dynamics to climate modeling. 7.2 Efficiency and Scalability Challenges Despite these successes, the quadratic complexity of standard attention with respect to sequence length remains a fundamental limitation. For sequences of lengthn, computing all pairwise attention scores re- quiresO(n 2) operations and memory, making it computationally prohibitive for very long contexts. This has motivated extensive research into efficient attention variants. Sparse attention patterns, as explored in Sparse Transformers [6] and Longformer [4], reduce complexity by restricting attention to local windows and selected global positions. These methods achieve linear or near-linear complexity while maintaining performance on tasks requiring long-range dependencies. Big Bird [34] combines local, global, and ran- dom attention patterns, proving theoretically that sparse attention can approximate full attention while dramatically reducing computational cost. Low-rank approximation methods offer another approach to efficiency. Linformer [32] projects keys and values to lower dimensions, reducing complexity toO(nk) wherek?n. Linear attention methods [21] and the Performer [7] use random feature approximations to estimate attention scores, achieving linear complex- ity through kernel methods. These approaches trade some expressiveness for computational efficiency, with empirical results suggesting the trade-off is often favorable. Recent work on Flash Attention [10] demon- strates that algorithmic optimizations exploiting hardware characteristics can yield substantial speedups without sacrificing accuracy. By carefully managing memory access patterns and leveraging GPU memory hierarchy, Flash Attention reduces memory reads/writes while computing exact attention, achieving 2-4x speedups over standard implementations. This highlights that implementation details matter as much as algorithmic complexity for practical performance. 7.3 Theoretical Understanding While the empirical success of Transformers is undeniable, the theoretical understanding of why and how they work remains incomplete. Recent theoretical work has begun addressing fundamental questions about Transformers' representational capacity and learning dynamics. Yun et al. [33] proved that Transformers 34 7.4. INTERPRETABILITY AND ANALYSIS 35 with sufficient depth can represent any continuous sequence-to-sequence function, establishing universal ap- proximation properties. However, these results require impractical depth, leaving open questions about what functions Transformers can efficiently learn in practice. Analysis of attention as performing similarity-based retrieval [13] provides intuition for how Transformers process information, but a rigorous characterization of learned representations remains challenging. Understanding training dynamics presents additional chal- lenges. The interplay between attention layers, feed-forward networks, and residual connections creates complex optimization landscapes. Recent work on neural tangent kernels for Transformers [18] provides some theoretical grounding, but the gap between infinite-width theory and finite practical models limits applicability. Developing a theory that explains phenomena like in-context learning, where models adapt to new tasks from examples in their input without gradient updates, represents an important frontier. 7.4 Interpretability and Analysis The attention weights in Transformers provide some interpretability, allowing inspection of which input positions influence each output. However, attention patterns often prove difficult to interpret meaningfully, particularly in deeper layers where representations become increasingly abstract. Research into Transformer interpretability has revealed both insights and limitations. Studies of attention patterns in trained mod- els [9] have identified specialized attention heads that attend to specific syntactic relationships in language tasks, suggesting some degree of interpretable structure. However, other work [19] demonstrates that at- tention weights do not always correspond to model behavior or feature importance, cautioning against over-interpreting attention as explanation. The distinction between attention as a mechanism and attention as explanation remains an active research question. Advances in mechanistic interpretability [13] aim to reverse-engineer learned algorithms in Transformers by analyzing internal representations and information flow. These approaches have successfully identified interpretable circuits for specific tasks, but scaling to large models trained on diverse data remains challenging. Developing robust methods for understanding, debugging, and controlling Transformer behavior represents a critical research direction for deploying these systems safely and reliably. 7.5 F uture Directions 7.5.1 Long-Context Modeling Extending Transformers to handle extremely long contexts efficiently remains an important goal. Applica- tions including book-length document understanding, long-form dialogue, and scientific literature analysis require processing sequences far exceeding current practical limits. Approaches combining hierarchical processing, memory mechanisms, and retrieval augmentation show promise for scaling to arbitrarily long contexts while maintaining computational tractability. 7.5.2 Multimodal Integration While attention has proven effective for multimodal learning, better methods for integrating diverse data types are needed. Cross-modal attention mechanisms that capture fine-grained alignments between vision and language [1] represent progress, but open questions remain about optimal architectures for three or more modalities, temporal alignment across modalities, and handling modality-specific structure. 7.5.3 Efficient Architectures Hybrid architectures combining Transformers with other mechanisms may offer better efficiency-performance trade-offs. State space models like S4 [15] achieve competitive performance with linear complexity by replacing attention with structured linear operators. Understanding when attention is necessary versus when alternatives suffice could enable more efficient architectures tailored to specific tasks. Mixture-of- Experts approaches [14] offer another path to scaling by activating only subsets of model parameters for each input. Combining sparse attention with sparse expert routing may enable models with trillions of parameters while maintaining manageable computational costs. 7.5.4 Continual and F ew-Shot Learning While Transformers exhibit impressive in-context learning, improving their ability to efficiently acquire and retain new knowledge remains important. Better understanding and enhancing few-shot learning capabili- ties could reduce data requirements for adapting models to specialized domains. Developing architectures 36 CHAPTER 7. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS that support continual learning without catastrophic forgetting while maintaining computational efficiency represents a key challenge. 7.5.5 Environmental Considerations The computational cost of training large Transformers raises important questions about energy consump- tion and environmental impact. Research into more efficient training methods, better transfer learning to reduce training from scratch, and specialized hardware for Transformer inference addresses these concerns. Developing metrics and best practices for sustainable AI development will become increasingly important as models scale. 7.6 Concluding Remarks Attention mechanisms have transformed artificial intelligence by providing a flexible, powerful framework for modeling relationships in sequential and structured data. The mathematical foundations developed in this monograph establish the theoretical basis for understanding these mechanisms, while highlighting open questions and challenges. As research addresses efficiency, theoretical understanding, interpretability, and domain-specific applications, attention-based architectures will continue evolving. Whether through improved Transformer variants, hybrid approaches combining multiple mechanisms, or entirely new archi- tectures inspired by attention principles, the core insight of learned, adaptive aggregation will remain central to progress in machine learning. The next decade promises continued innovation, building on the attention paradigm established over the past several years. The OOM results for standard Transformer occur during training when maintaining consistent batch sizes across all sequence lengths for fair comparison. With standard data parallelism, each GPU maintains a complete copy of the model, optimizer states, and gradients; thus, the 840GB = 320GB total memory cannot be pooled, and each GPU independently faces the 40GB memory constraint. The quadratic memory footprint includes: (1) the attention matrices (approximately 32GB per layer for batch size of 16 at 8192 tokens with mixed precision), (2) activation storage for backpropagation, (3) optimizer states (Adam requires 2 parameter memory), and (4) gradient accumulation. While it is possible to train longer sequences with reduced batch size or gradient checkpointing, we maintain consistent training configurations across all models for fair efficiency comparison. CPA demonstrates excellent scalability, with memory usage and computation time scaling linearly with sequence length. For short sequences (512 tokens), the efficiency gains are moderate compared to standard Transformers. However, as sequence length increases, the benefits become increasingly pronounced. At 8,192 tokens, standard Transformers run out of memory (OOM) on our hardware, while CPA continues to function efficiently. At 32,768 tokens, CPA maintains the lowest memory usage and highest inference speed among all compared models who went Out-Of-Memory. Figure 6 visualizes the scaling of memory usage with respect to sequence length, clearly showing the quadratic scaling of standard Transformers versus the linear scaling of CPA and other efficient attention variants. Analysis of learned attention patterns To better understand how CPA allocates attention, we visualize the sparse attention weights for different layers and heads on the WMT14 En-De translation task. Figure 8 shows attention visualizations for representative heads in different layers. Fig. 8. Open in a new tab Visualization of learned attention patterns in CPA. Each colored bar represents a token receiving non-zero attention, with color intensity indicating attention weight magnitude. (a-c) show patterns from different layers and heads, demonstrating increasing specialization from early to deeper layers. (d) shows average attention by position across all heads in the final layer. We observe several interesting patterns: Specialization by head: Different attention heads focus on different aspects of the input. Some heads attend primarily to content words (nouns, verbs), while others focus on function words or syntactic markers. Layer-specific behavior: Early layers (Figure 8a) tend to have more distributed attention, while deeper layers (Figure 8c) become increasingly focused on specific tokens that are semantically important for the current context. Context-dependent sparsity: The number of tokens receiving non-zero attention varies significantly based on the input complexity. Simple sentences result in very sparse attention (5-10% of tokens), while complex sentences with ambiguous references or specialized terminology lead to less sparse patterns (20-30% of tokens). Positional biases: Despite not explicitly encoding positional relationships in the attention mechanism, certain heads develop positional biases (Figure 8d), focusing on tokens near the beginning or end of the sequence. These observations suggest that CPA learns meaningful attention allocation strategies that adapt to input complexity, supporting our hypothesis that explicit pairwise comparisons are often redundant. Discussion Key findings Our experimental results demonstrate that Contextual Priority Attention achieves performance competitive with standard self-attention while significantly reducing computational costs. This supports our hypothesis that explicit pairwise token interactions may be unnecessary for effective contextual modeling. The global-to-local attention paradigm of CPA offers several advantages: Efficiency: Linear scaling with sequence length enables processing of much longer sequences than standard Transformers can handle. Our results show CPA can efficiently process sequences up to 32K tokens, where standard Transformers run out of memory. Interpretability: The sparse attention patterns highlight which tokens are most contextually relevant, providing insights into model decision-making. As shown in our analysis of attention patterns, CPA learns meaningful token prioritization strategies. Adaptivity: The number of tokens attended to naturally adapts to input complexity, allocating computational resources where needed. This results in more efficient processing of simple inputs while maintaining capacity for complex ones. Effectiveness on long sequences: CPA performs particularly well on long document tasks, where capturing both local and global context is essential. This makes it well-suited for applications like document-level machine translation, long-form question answering, and document summarization. Figure 9 illustrates the performance-complexity trade-off for different attention mechanisms. CPA achieves an attractive balance, delivering near-standard-Transformer performance with linear computational complexity. Fig. 9. Open in a new tab Performance vs. computational complexity for different attention mechanisms on the WMT14 En-De translation task. The ideal models would be in the top-left corner (high performance, low complexity). CPA achieves a favorable trade-off, approaching the performance of standard Transformers while maintaining linear complexity. Limitations Despite its promising results, CPA has several limitations that present opportunities for future research: Global context quality: The performance of CPA depends critically on the quality of the Global Context Vector. For very complex or ambiguous inputs, a single context vector may not capture all relevant aspects of the sequence. This limitation becomes more pronounced as sequence length increases beyond the sizes tested in our experiments. Task-specific performance: While CPA performs well across most tasks, it shows slightly lower performance on certain language modeling benchmarks. This suggests that some tasks may benefit more from exhaustive pairwise comparisons. Training dynamics: We observed that CPA models sometimes require more careful initialization and training compared to standard Transformers, likely due to the increased importance of the global context representation. Learning meaningful global representations early in training is crucial for model convergence. Theoretical capacity: While we prove that CPA can theoretically approximate standard attention, this approximation may require higher model capacity in practice. Our experiments compensated for this by slightly increasing the hidden dimensions in the priority scoring MLP. Hardware utilization: The sparse attention patterns in CPA, while theoretically efficient, may not fully utilize modern GPU hardware designed for dense matrix operations. Custom CUDA kernels for sparse operations help mitigate this issue but introduce additional implementation complexity. Future directions Our work opens several promising directions for future research: Hierarchical CPA: Creating hierarchical representations of global context at different granularities could help capture both fine-grained and high-level patterns. This approach would involve computing multiple context vectors at different levels of abstraction, from local windows to global document-level representations. Adaptive sparsity: Dynamically adjusting the sparsity level based on input complexity could further improve efficiency without sacrificing performance. This could be implemented by learning a threshold function that determines the minimum attention weight required for a token to be considered relevant. Causal CPA for auto-regressive generation: Our current implementation applies CPA only in encoder architectures. Extending CPA to efficient causal decoding in decoder-only models (like GPT-style architectures) requires careful design to handle incremental GCV updates. One promising approach is to maintain a running GCV that can be updated in time per generated token: . This would enable linear-time auto-regressive generation while maintaining the benefits of global context-driven attention. Cross-modal applications: The global context approach may be particularly well-suited for cross-modal attention, where different modalities (text, image, audio) require different attention patterns. For example, in multimodal tasks, separate global context vectors could be computed for each modality, then used to guide cross-modal attention. Theoretical exploration: Further theoretical analysis of the expressivity-efficiency tradeoff in different attention mechanisms could guide the development of even more efficient variants. This includes a deeper understanding of what types of dependencies can be captured by global-context-based attention versus explicit pairwise attention. Pre-training and transfer learning: Investigating how CPA performs in large-scale pre-training scenarios and subsequent fine-tuning could reveal its potential for more efficient foundation models. The linear scaling properties of CPA make it particularly promising for very large models trained on extensive datasets. Hardware optimization: CPA's sparse attention patterns could enable specialized hardware implementations for even greater efficiency gains. Future research could explore hardware designs specifically optimized for global-context-based sparse attention mechanisms. Figure 10 illustrates these potential future directions, highlighting their relative complexity and potential impact. We believe the hierarchical CPA and adaptive sparsity approaches represent the most immediate opportunities for significant improvements. Fig. 10. Open in a new tab Potential future directions for extending Contextual Priority Attention. Each path represents a promising avenue for research, with estimated complexity and potential impact. Conclusion We presented Contextual Priority Attention (CPA), a novel attention mechanism that achieves theoretical complexity while empirically demonstrating linear scaling and maintaining competitive performance with standard Transformers. By reimagining attention as a global-context-driven priority system rather than exhaustive pairwise comparisons, CPA offers significant efficiency improvements, particularly for long sequences. Our experimental results across diverse tasks demonstrate that CPA achieves performance comparable to full attention while scaling more efficiently to long inputs. The emergent attention patterns reveal that CPA learns meaningful prioritization strategies that adapt to input complexity. On the Long Range Arena benchmark specifically designed to test long-range modeling capabilities, CPA outperforms other efficient attention variants by a significant margin. The success of CPA suggests that the quadratic computational complexity of standard self-attention may be unnecessary for effective contextual modeling. By focusing computational resources on the most contextually relevant tokens, CPA provides an efficient alternative that scales better to the increasingly long contexts required by modern NLP applications. The ability to process sequences of tens of thousands of tokens efficiently opens up new possibilities for applications such as document-level translation, long-form question answering, and full-document summarization. Source: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2009.14794 URL: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2009.14794 Task: q007 Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2021 RETHINKING ATTENTION WITH PERFORMERS Krzysztof Choromanski?1, Valerii Likhosherstov?2, David Dohan?1, Xingyou Song?1 Andreea Gane?1, Tamas Sarlos?1, Peter Hawkins?1, Jared Davis?3, Afroz Mohiuddin1 Lukasz Kaiser1, David Belanger1, Lucy Colwell1,2, Adrian Weller2,4 1Google 2University of Cambridge 3DeepMind 4Alan Turing Institute ABSTRACT We introduce Performers, Transformer architectures which can estimate regular (softmax) full-rank-attention Transformers with provable accuracy, but using only linear (as opposed to quadratic) space and time complexity, without relying on any priors such as sparsity or low-rankness. To approximate softmax attention- kernels, Performers use a novel Fast Attention Via positive Orthogonal Random features approach (FA VOR+), which may be of independent interest for scalable kernel methods. FA VOR+ can also be used to ef?ciently model kernelizable attention mechanisms beyond softmax. This representational power is crucial to accurately compare softmax with other kernels for the ?rst time on large-scale tasks, beyond the reach of regular Transformers, and investigate optimal attention-kernels. Performers are linear architectures fully compatible with regular Transformers and with strong theoretical guarantees: unbiased or nearly-unbiased estimation of the attention matrix, uniform convergence and low estimation variance. We tested Performers on a rich set of tasks stretching from pixel-prediction through text models to protein sequence modeling. We demonstrate competitive results with other examined ef?cient sparse and dense attention methods, showcasing effectiveness of the novel attention-learning paradigm leveraged by Performers. 1 I NTRODUCTION AND RELATED WORK Transformers (Vaswani et al., 2017; Dehghani et al., 2019) are powerful neural network architectures that have become SOTA in several areas of machine learning including natural language processing (NLP) (e.g. speech recognition (Luo et al., 2020)), neural machine translation (NMT) (Chen et al., 2018), document generation/summarization, time series prediction, generative modeling (e.g. image generation (Parmar et al., 2018)), music generation (Huang et al., 2019), and bioinformatics (Rives et al., 2019; Madani et al., 2020; Ingraham et al., 2019; Elnaggar et al., 2019; Du et al., 2020). Transformers rely on a trainable attention mechanism that identi?es complex dependencies between the elements of each input sequence. Unfortunately, the regular Transformer scales quadratically with the number of tokens L in the input sequence, which is prohibitively expensive for large L and precludes its usage in settings with limited computational resources even for moderate values ofL. Several solutions have been proposed to address this issue (Beltagy et al., 2020; Gulati et al., 2020; Chan et al., 2020; Child et al., 2019; Bello et al., 2019). Most approaches restrict the attention mechanism to attend to local neighborhoods (Parmar et al., 2018) or incorporate structural priors on attention such as sparsity (Child et al., 2019), pooling-based compression (Rae et al., 2020) clustering/binning/convolution techniques (e.g. (Roy et al., 2020) which appliesk-means clustering to learn dynamic sparse attention regions, or (Kitaev et al., 2020), where locality sensitive hashing is used to group together tokens of similar embeddings), sliding windows (Beltagy et al., 2020), or truncated targeting (Chelba et al., 2020). There is also a long line of research on using dense attention matrices, but de?ned by low-rank kernels substituting softmax (Katharopoulos et al., 2020; Shen et al., 2018). Those methods critically rely on kernels admitting explicit representations as dot-products of ?nite positive-feature vectors. The approaches above do not aim to approximate regular attention, but rather propose simpler and more tractable attention mechanisms, often by incorporating additional constraints (e.g. identical query and key sets as in (Kitaev et al., 2020)), or by trading regular with sparse attention using more ?Equal contribution. Correspondence to {kchoro,lcolwell}@google.com. Code for Transformer models on protein data can be found in github.com/google-research/ google-research/tree/master/protein_lm and Performer code can be found in github.com/ google-research/google-research/tree/master/performer. Google AI Blog: https:// ai.googleblog.com/2020/10/rethinking-attention-with-performers.html 1 arXiv:2009.14794v4 [cs.LG] 19 Nov 2022 Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2021 layers (Child et al., 2019). Unfortunately, there is a lack of rigorous guarantees for the representation power produced by such methods, and sometimes the validity of sparsity patterns can only be veri?ed empirically through trial and error by constructing special GPU operations (e.g. either writing C++ CUDA kernels (Child et al., 2019) or using TVMs (Beltagy et al., 2020)). Other techniques which aim to reduce Transformers' space complexity include reversible residual layers allowing one-time activation storage in training (Kitaev et al., 2020) and shared attention weights (Xiao et al., 2019). These constraints may impede application to long-sequence problems, where approximations of the attention mechanism are not suf?cient. Approximations based on truncated back-propagation (Dai et al., 2019) are also unable to capture long-distance correlations since the gradients are only propagated inside a localized window. Other methods propose biased estimation of regular attention but only in the non-causal setting and with large mean squared error (Wang et al., 2020). In response, we introduce the ?rst Transformer architectures, Performers, capable of provably accurate and practical estimation of regular (softmax) full-rank attention, but of only linear space and time complexity and not relying on any priors such as sparsity or low-rankness. Performers use the Fast Attention Via positive Orthogonal Random features(FA VOR+) mechanism, leveraging new methods for approximating softmax and Gaussian kernels, which we propose. We believe these methods are of independent interest, contributing to the theory of scalable kernel methods. Consequently, Performers are the ?rst linear architectures fully compatible (via small amounts of ?ne-tuning) with regular Transformers, providing strong theoretical guarantees: unbiased or nearly-unbiased estimation of the attention matrix, uniform convergence and lower variance of the approximation. FA VOR+ can be also applied to ef?ciently model other kernelizable attention mechanisms beyond softmax. This representational power is crucial to accurately compare softmax with other kernels for the ?rst time on large-scale tasks, that are beyond the reach of regular Transformers, and ?nd for them optimal attention-kernels. FA VOR+ can also be applied beyond the Transformer scope as a more scalable replacement for regular attention, which itself has a wide variety of uses in computer vision (Fu et al., 2019), reinforcement learning (Zambaldi et al., 2019), training with softmax cross entropy loss, and even combinatorial optimization (Vinyals et al., 2015). We test Performers on a rich set of tasks ranging from pixel-prediction through text models to protein sequence modeling. We demonstrate competitive results with other examined ef?cient sparse and dense attention methods, showcasing the effectiveness of the novel attention-learning paradigm leveraged by Performers. We emphasize that in principle, FA VOR+ can also be combined with other techniques, such as reversible layers (Kitaev et al., 2020) or cluster-based attention (Roy et al., 2020). 2 FAVOR+ M ECHANISM & POSITIVE ORTHOGONAL RANDOM FEATURES Below we describe in detail the FA VOR+ mechanism - the backbone of thePerformer?s architecture. Incorporating positional information To maintain the Transformer's ability to model sequence order, we incorporate positional information by adding positional encodings to the input embeddings before computing the GCV and priority scores: 11 where is the positional encoding for position i, implemented using either the sinusoidal encodings from Vaswani et al.1 or learned positional embeddings. Theoretical analysis In this section, we analyze the theoretical properties of Contextual Priority Attention, particularly its relationship to standard self-attention and its capacity to model dependencies in sequential data. Relationship to standard self-attention Standard self-attention computes attention weights as: 12 where are the query and key vectors for tokens i and j, respectively. We can show that under certain conditions, CPA approximates this pairwise attention mechanism. Specifically, if our priority scoring function is structured as: 13 where is a weighted sum of all key vectors (our Global Context Vector), then CPA implicitly captures pairwise interactions through this shared context. Proposition 1 Let be the attention matrix from standard self-attention, and let be the attention weights from CPA. If the GCV is computed as with weights proportional to the importance of token j in the sequence, then there exists a parameterization of the priority scoring function such that 14 The proof is provided in Appendix . The key insight is that CPA's prioritization based on global context provides an efficient proxy for explicit token-to-token attention when the context sufficiently represents the relevant aspects of all tokens. Expressive power A natural question is whether CPA can express the same functions as standard self-attention. We prove that: Theorem 1 For any self-attention mechanism with weights , there exists a parameterization of CPA that can approximate the function computed by this self-attention mechanism to arbitrary precision, provided the dimension of the Global Context Vector is sufficiently large. The proof, outlined in Appendix, relies on the universal approximation capabilities of neural networks30 and the fact that our priority scoring MLP can learn to extract token-specific queries from the global context. With sufficient capacity, the priority scoring function can learn to attend to the same tokens that would receive high attention weights in the standard mechanism. Practical implementation: While Theorem 1 is an existence proof establishing that CPA can theoretically approximate standard attention with a sufficiently large GCV, in our experiments we use a GCV of dimension (i.e., the same as the model dimension). This choice: Does not grow with sequence length n, maintaining constant parameter count Matches the dimensionality of keys and queries in standard Transformers Empirically provides sufficient representational capacity for all tested tasks (section "Results and analysis") The theorem's "sufficient capacity" condition is satisfied by the MLP's hidden dimension ( in our experiments) rather than by increasing the GCV dimension. We found no benefit from using even for sequences up to 32K tokens. While this theoretical result establishes that CPA has the expressive capacity to approximate standard attention, in practice, the inductive biases of the two approaches differ significantly, leading to different learning dynamics and generalization properties. Complexity-expressivity tradeoff We analyze the tradeoff between computational complexity and model expressivity for different attention variants: Standard self-attention: complexity, full expressivity. Linear attention (e.g., Performers): complexity, reduced expressivity due to kernel approximation. Pattern-based sparse attention: complexity where , limited by fixed patterns. CPA (our approach): theoretical complexity with experimentally observed linear scaling, expressivity modulated by GCV capacity. Figure 4 visualizes this tradeoff for various attention mechanisms. Unlike kernel-based methods, CPA doesn't rely on specific mathematical properties of the attention function. Instead, it learns to extract and use relevant global context, potentially capturing higher-order interactions that aren't easily expressible with fixed kernels. Fig. 4. Open in a new tab Theoretical trade-off between computational complexity and expressivity for different attention mechanisms. The arrow indicates the ideal direction (lower complexity, higher expressivity). CPA achieves a favorable balance by maintaining linear complexity while preserving much of the expressivity of standard attention. Information bottleneck perspective The Global Context Vector in CPA can be viewed through the lens of the Information Bottleneck (IB) principle25. The GCV creates a compressed representation of the input sequence, retaining the most relevant information while discarding noise. Proposition 2 Under the Information Bottleneck framework, the optimal Global Context Vector is one that maximizes , where denotes mutual information, is the input sequence, Y is the target output, and controls the compression-relevance tradeoff. This perspective provides theoretical justification for why CPA works well: it implicitly performs a form of information bottleneck, focusing on the most task-relevant aspects of the input sequence while filtering out irrelevant details. Experimental setup We evaluate CPA on a diverse set of tasks to assess its performance across different domains and sequence lengths. Our evaluation focuses on comparing CPA against standard self-attention and state-of-the-art efficient attention mechanisms. Model configurations CPA application in different architectures For encoder-decoder tasks (machine translation, summarization), we apply CPA to replace self-attention in the encoder only. The decoder employs standard masked self-attention for auto-regressive generation and standard cross-attention to attend to encoder outputs. This design choice offers several advantages: The encoder's Global Context Vector is computed once for the entire source sequence and remains fixed during decoding, ensuring efficient inference. The decoder's standard attention preserves the ability to attend to all previously generated tokens without modification. Cross-attention maintains full expressivity for encoder-decoder alignment. For encoder-only tasks (classification, language modeling with fixed context), CPA replaces all self-attention layers. For all model variants, we keep other components (feed-forward networks, layer normalization, residual connections) unchanged. Developing an efficient causal variant of CPA for decoder-only auto-regressive models is a promising direction for future work, which we discuss in section "Future directions". For fair comparison, we maintain the same model size (number of parameters) across all compared models by appropriately adjusting the hidden dimensions. We consider four variants of our approach: CPA-Avg: Using learned weighted averaging for GCV CPA-CLS: Using a [CLS] token approach for GCV CPA-CNN: Using a convolutional network with global pooling for GCV CPA-BERT: A BERT-style model with CPA replacing self-attention For all CPA variants, we use the two-layer MLP priority scoring function with hidden dimension , and the sparsemax transformation for sparse attention allocation unless otherwise specified. Baselines We compare against the following baselines: Standard Transformer1: The original Transformer with full self-attention Sparse Transformer2: Uses fixed sparse attention patterns Longformer8: Combines local windowed attention with global tokens Linformer4: Uses low-rank approximation of attention Performer5: Uses kernel-based approximation Reformer3: Uses locality-sensitive hashing BigBird10: Combines random, global, and local attention patterns We use the official implementations of these baselines with their recommended configurations, adjusting model sizes to match parameter counts for fair comparison. Tasks and datasets We evaluate on the following tasks and datasets: Machine translation: WMT14 English-German (En-De): 4.5M sentence pairs, evaluated with BLEU score WMT14 English-French (En-Fr): 36M sentence pairs, evaluated with BLEU score Language modeling: WikiText-10331: 103M tokens from Wikipedia articles, evaluated with perplexity PG1932: 28K books from Project Gutenberg, evaluated with perplexity Long document classification: Long Range Arena (LRA) benchmark33: A suite of tasks designed to test the ability to handle long-range dependencies IMDB Movie Reviews34: 50K movie reviews for sentiment analysis Hyperpartisan News Detection35: Articles labeled as hyperpartisan or not Question answering: SQuAD v1.1 and v2.036,37: Stanford Question Answering Dataset Natural Questions (NQ)38: Questions from real Google search queries TriviaQA39: Question-answer pairs from trivia competitions Long-context generation: CNN/Daily Mail summarization40: News articles with abstractive summaries arXiv paper summarization41: Scientific papers with abstracts as summaries Implementation details Our implementation is based on PyTorch42 and the HuggingFace Transformers library43. The sparse transformations (sparsemax and top-k Gumbel-Softmax) are implemented using custom CUDA kernels for efficiency. We employ mixed-precision training using NVIDIA Apex for all experiments. For machine translation tasks, we follow the standard Transformer base configuration1 with 6 encoder and 6 decoder layers, 8 attention heads, and 512-dimensional embeddings. For other tasks, we adjust model size according to task complexity and dataset size, ensuring fair comparison across all models. Detailed model configurations for each task are provided in Appendix. Training details We train all models using the Adam optimizer44 with a transformer-standard learning rate schedule: 15 We use label smoothing of 0.1 for classification tasks and dropout with probability 0.1 for all layers. Models are trained on 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs with mixed precision training. For each task, we select hyperparameters based on validation performance. We employ early stopping based on validation performance with a patience of 10 epochs. To ensure reproducibility, we use five different random seeds for each experiment and report the mean and standard deviation of the results. Evaluation metrics We use task-specific evaluation metrics: BLEU scores for machine translation, computed using SacreBLEU451 to ensure reproducibility and fair comparison with prior work Perplexity for language modeling Accuracy for classification tasks F1 and Exact Match scores for question answering ROUGE scores (R-1, R-2, R-L) for summarization Additionally, we measure: Training time (hours) Peak memory usage (GB) Inference speed (tokens/second) FLOPs per sequence Model parameter count All runtime and memory measurements are conducted on identical hardware configurations to ensure fair comparison. For brevity, we report results for the best-performing CPA variant (CPA-Avg) in the main table and provide detailed comparisons between all CPA variants in Appendix. Table 2. Our findings indicate that CPA achieves competitive performance with standard Transformers across all tasks, with performance differences generally within 0.5 points. Among efficient attention variants, CPA-Avg consistently achieves strong results, ranking as first or second-best among efficient attention methods on all benchmarks. On tasks involving long sequences (LRA benchmark and document summarization), CPA demonstrates particularly strong results, outperforming most efficient attention alternatives by a significant margin. This suggests that our global-context approach effectively captures long-range dependencies without requiring quadratic computation. Figure 5 shows detailed performance on the Long Range Arena benchmark, which specifically tests models' ability to handle long sequences. CPA excels on tasks requiring long-range modeling, such as the Text and Retrieval subtasks, while maintaining competitive performance on other subtasks. Fig. 5. Chapter 3 Self-Attention Mechanisms Self-attention represents a fundamental innovation in which a sequence attends to itself, allowing each position to gather information from all positions in the same sequence. This mechanism forms the core of the Transformer architecture and enables modeling of complex intra-sequence dependencies. 3.1 Definition and F ormulation Unlike traditional attention mechanisms that operate between distinct source and target sequences (e.g., encoder and decoder in machine translation), self-attention computes attention within a single sequence. Chapter 4 Multi-Head Attention A single attention mechanism may be limited in its capacity to capture different types of relationships simultaneously. Multi-head attention addresses this limitation by computing multiple attention functions in parallel, each with independent parameters, allowing the model to attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions. 4.1 Motivation and Architecture Consider the task of understanding the sentence "The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired." The pronoun "it" could potentially refer to either "animal" or "street," though in this context it refers to "animal." Determining this requires understanding: 1. Syntactic structure (subject-verb relationships) 2. Semantic plausibility (animals get tired, streets don't) 3. Long-range dependencies (the pronoun appears far from its antecedent) A single attention mechanism must balance these different types of information. Multi-head attention allows different heads to specialize in different aspects, some focusing on syntax, others on semantics, others on positional patterns. 4.1.1 F ormal Definition Definition 4.1(Multi-Head Attention).Multi-head attention withhheads computeshparallel attention functions, each with separate parameters, then concatenates and linearly projects the results. Additional Ef?ciency Techniques Several additional techniques can be introduced on top of Linformer to further optimize for both performance and ef?ciency: Parameter sharing between projections: One can share parameters for the linear projection matri- cesEi,Fi across layers and heads. In particular, we experimented with 3 levels of sharing: ? Headwise sharing: for each layer, we share two projection matrices E andF such that Ei =E andFi =F across all headsi. ? Key-value sharing: we do headwise sharing, with the additional constraint of sharing the key and value projections. For each layer, we create a single projection matrixE such that Ei =Fi =E for each key-value projection matrix across all headi. ? Layerwise sharing: we use a single projection matrix E across all layers, for all heads, and for both key and value. For example, in a 12-layer, 12-head stacked Transformer model, headwise sharing, key-value sharing and layerwise sharing will introduce 24, 12, and 1 distinct linear projection matrices, respectively. Nonuniform projected dimension: One can choose a different projected dimensionk for different heads and layers. As shown in Figure 1 (right), the contextual mapping matrices in different heads and layers have distinct spectrum distributions, and heads in higher layer tend towards a more skewed distributed spectrum (lower rank). This implies one can choose a smaller projected dimensionk for higher layers. General projections: One can also choose different kinds of low-dimensional projection methods instead of a simple linear projection. For example, one can choose mean/max pooling, or convolution where the kernel and stride is set ton/k. The convolutional functions contain parameters that require training. 5 Experiments In this section, we present experimental results for the the techniques described above. In this paper, we demonstrate, both theoretically and empirically, that the stochastic matrix formed by self-attention mechanism is low-rank. We further leverage this observation to propose a new, highly ef?cient self- attention mechanism. Through a combination of theoretical and empirical analysis, we demonstrate that our proposed approach isO(n) with respect to sequence length. Broader Impact Our work focuses on making Transformers more ef?cient by introducing a mechanism that reduces self-attention to linear-time complexity. Potential positive impacts of ef?cient transformers include increasing the accessibility of our models, both for deployment on devices, as well as during training for research purposes. It also has potential impact on training transformer on images since we can support very long sequences. School of EECS Queen Mary University of London London, UK s.hosseini@qmul.ac.uk Abstract Scaled Dot Product Attention (SDPA) is the backbone of many modern deep- learning models. It is so versatile that it has been used in natural language, vision, and multi-modal domains with very little change compared to its original formula- tion. This paper discusses why the current formulation is inefficient by delving into the mathematical details of the attention mechanism. We propose three improve- ments to mitigate these inefficiencies, thereby, introducing three enhanced attention mechanisms: Optimised, Efficient, and Super Attention. Optimised and Efficient Attention have one and two matrix multiplications fewer per head, respectively, and 25% and 50% fewer parameters, respectively, than standard SDPA, but perform similarly to standard SDPA in both vision and natural language tasks. They can be used in all applications where SDPA is used while offering smaller model sizes and faster training and inference without noticeable loss in performance. Super Attention introduces a new linear transformation on the values, transforming them from the left. It outperforms standard SPDA on vision and natural language tasks by up to 17% while having one fewer matrix multiplication per head and 25% fewer parameters than standard SDPA. Consequently, it is also faster than standard SDPA. Super Attention is ideal in applications where the attention layer's context length is fixed, such as Vision Transformers. In addition to providing mathematical reasoning, we evaluate the presented attention mechanisms on several datasets including MNIST, CIFAR100, ImageNet, IMDB Movie Reviews, and Amazon Reviews datasets, as well as combined Europarl and Anki English-Spanish datasets for neural machine translation. 1 Introduction Not many ideas have had as profound an effect on the field of Artificial Intelligence (AI) as the attention mechanism (Bahdanau et al., 2015). Introduced as a method to improve machine translation, the attention mechanism revolutionised the way neural networks process and interpret data. By allowing models to focus on specific parts of the input while disregarding irrelevant information, it mimics a form of cognitive attention in humans. It not only enhanced the capability and efficiency of Language Models (LM) but also paved the way for the development of advanced AI architectures like the Transformer model (Vaswani et al., 2017). These advances have had far-reaching impacts, extending beyond Natural Language Processing (NLP) to other areas such as image recognition (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021), autonomous systems (Mott et al., 2019), healthcare (Choi et al., 2016), and multi-modal application Xu et al. The formulation of SDPA in all these domains has undergone very little change compared to the original formulation of Vaswani et al. (2017). Instead, "The bigger the better" has been the prevailing maxim in AI in the last few years. Larger Language Models (LLM), such as Llama 3 (Touvron et al., 2023a,b), GPT-4 (Achiam et al., 2023), and Gemini (Anil et al., 2023) have demonstrated unprecedented capabilities in multi-modal domains. The behemothic sizes of these models have introduced numerous challenges, such as expensive and slow training and inference, leading to secondary problems such as high carbon emission (Dhar, 2020). Furthermore, such models are impossible not only to run but even to store on edge devices such as smartphones, consumer laptops, and even powerful personal workstations. In recent years, there have been numerous attempts to address this problem using post-training techniques, like quantisation (Jacob et al., 2018), Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) (Hu et al., 2022), Quantised LoRA (QLoRA) (Dettmers et al., 2023), and sparsification (Ashkboos et al., 2024). There have been also attempts to optimise the speed and GPU utilisation of attention-based models. Notable examples include Flash Attention Dao et al. (2022) and its successor, Flash Attention 2 Dao (2024). All these approaches focus on techniques to improve the performance of attention-based models without altering the attention mechanism. In this paper, we look into the attention mechanism itself and put forward three attention mechanisms, Optimised Attention, Efficient Attention, and Super Attention. Our contributions are founded on two intuitive principles: 1. Two consecutive linear transformations result in a linear transformation. 2. A linear kernel between each input increases learning. Using Principle 1, Optimised Attention omits the values' linear transformation, (see Fig. 1b and Eq. (4)) while preserving the learning capabilities. We use Principle 1 once more in Efficient Attention to not only omit the values' linear transformation but also that of the keys (see Fig. 1c and Eq. (5)). Finally, Super Attention uses Principle 2 and introduces a new learnable kernel W A in between the attention scores and values (see Fig. 1d and Eq. (22)), thus enhancing the performance of SDPA in both vision and NLP tasks compared to standard attention, while being more efficient and having fewer parameters. We validate our proposed algorithms on image classification on MNIST, CIFAR100, and ImageNet datasets, natural language sentiment classification on IMDB and Amazon Reviews datasets, and Neural Machine Translation (NMT) on the combined Europarl and Anki English-to-Spanish translation dataset. Published 05 December 2024 By Dave Bergmann and Cole Stryker What is an attention mechanism? An attention mechanism is a machine learning technique that directs deep learning models to prioritize (or attend to) the most relevant parts of input data. Innovation in attention mechanisms enabled the transformer architecture that yielded the modern large language models (LLMs) that power popular applications like ChatGPT. As their name suggests, attention mechanisms are inspired by the ability of humans (and other animals) to selectively pay more attention to salient details and ignore details that are less important in the moment. Having access to all information but focusing on only the most relevant information helps to ensure that no meaningful details are lost while enabling efficient use of limited memory and time. Mathematically speaking, an attention mechanism computes attention weights that reflect the relative importance of each part of an input sequence to the task at hand. It then applies those attention weights to increase (or decrease) the influence of each part of the input, in accordance with its respective importance. An attention model-that is, an artificial intelligence model that employs an attention mechanism-is trained to assign accurate attention weights through supervised learning or self-supervised learning on a large dataset of examples. Attention mechanisms were originally introduced by Bahdanau et al in 2014 as a technique to address the shortcomings of what were then state-of-the-art recurrent neural network (RNN) models used for machine translation. Subsequent research integrated attention mechanisms into the convolutional neural networks (CNNs) used for tasks such as image captioning and visual question answering. In 2017, the seminal paper "Attention is All You Need" introduced the transformer model, which eschews recurrence and convolutions altogether in favor of only attention layers and standard feedforward layers. The transformer architecture has since become the backbone of the cutting-edge models powering the ongoing era of generative AI. While attention mechanisms are primarily associated with LLMs used for natural language processing (NLP) tasks, such as summarization, question answering, text generation and sentiment analysis, attention-based models are also used widely in other domains. Leading diffusion models used for image generation often incorporate an attention mechanism. In the field of computer vision, vision transformers (ViTs) have achieved superior results on tasks including object detection,1 image segmentation2 and visual question answering.3 Join 100,000+ subscribers for the latest tech news Stay up to date on the most important-and intriguing-industry news on AI, automation, data, quantum, infrastructure and security with the Think Newsletter, delivered twice weekly. Why are attention mechanisms important? Transformer models and the attention mechanisms that power them have achieved state-of-the-art results across nearly every subdomain of deep learning. The nature of attention mechanisms gives them significant advantages over the convolution mechanisms used in convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and recurrent loops used in recurrent neural networks (RNNs). Flexibility over time: The way RNNs process sequential data is inherently serialized, meaning that they process each timestep in a sequence individually in a specific order. This makes it difficult for an RNN to discern correlations-called dependencies, in the parlance of data science-that have many steps in between them. Attention mechanisms, conversely, can examine an entire sequence simultaneously and make decisions about the order in which to focus on specific steps. Flexibility over space: CNNs are inherently local, using convolutions to process smaller subsets of input data one piece at a time. This makes it difficult for a CNN to discern dependencies that are far apart, such as correlations between words (in text) or pixels (in images) that aren't neighboring one another. Attention mechanisms don't have this limitation, as they process data in an entirely different way. Parallelization: The nature of attention mechanisms entails many computational steps being done at once, rather than in a serialized manner. This, in turns, enables a high degree of parallel computing, taking advantage of the power and speed offered by GPUs. To understand how attention mechanisms in deep learning work and why they helped spark a revolution in generative AI, it helps to first understand why attention was first introduced: to improve the RNN-based Seq2Seq models used for machine translation. How Seq2Seq works without attention mechanisms RNNs are neural networks with recurrent loops that provide an equivalent of "memory," enabling them to process sequential data. RNNs intake an ordered sequence of input vectors and process them in timesteps. After each timestep, the resulting network state-called the hidden state-is provided back to the loop, along with the next input vector. RNNs quickly suffer from vanishing or exploding gradients in training. This made RNNs impractical for many NLP tasks, as it greatly limited the length of input sentences they could process.4 These limitations were somewhat mitigated by an improved RNN architecture called long short term memory networks (LSTMs), which add gating mechanisms to preserve "long term" memory. Before attention was introduced, the Seq2Seq model was the state-of-the-art model for machine translation. Seq2Seq uses two LSTMs in an encoder-decoder architecture. The first LSTM, the encoder, processes the source sentence step by step, then outputs the hidden state of the final timestep. This output, the context vector, encodes the whole sentence as one vector embedding. To enable Seq2Seq to flexibly handle sentences with varying numbers of word, the context vector is always the same length. The second LSTM, the decoder, takes the vector embedding output by the encoder as its initial input and decodes it, word by word, into a second language. Encoding input sequences in a fixed number of dimensions allowed Seq2Seq to process sequences of varying length, but also introduced important flaws: It represents long or complex sequences with the same level of detail as shorter, simpler sentences. This causes an information bottleneck for longer sequences and wastes resources for shorter sequences. This vector represents only the final hidden state of the encoder network. In theory, each subsequent hidden state should contain information provided by the previous hidden state, which in turn contains information from the prior time step, and so on, back to the first step. In practice, the context vector inevitably "forgets" information from early time steps, hindering model performance on lengthier sequences. How attention mechanisms improved Seq2Seq Bahdanau et al proposed an attention mechanism in their 2014 paper, "Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate," to improve communication between the encoder and decoder and remove that information bottleneck. Instead of passing along only the final hidden state of the encoder-the context vector-to the decoder, their model passed every encoder hidden state to the decoder. The attention mechanism itself was used to determine which hidden state-that is, which word in the original sentence-was most relevant at each translation step performed by the decoder. "This frees the model from having to encode a whole source sentence into a fixed-length vector, and also lets the model focus only on information relevant to the generation of the next target word," the paper explained. "This has a major positive impact on the ability of the neural machine translation system to yield good results on longer sentences."5 Subsequent NLP research focused primarily on improving performance and expanding use cases for attention mechanisms in recurrent models. The 2017 invention of transformer models, powered solely by attention, eventually made RNNs all but obsolete for NLP. New episodes on Fridays at 6 AM EST. Go to episodes How do attention mechanisms work? An attention mechanism's primary purpose is to determine the relative importance of different parts of the input sequence, then influence the model to attend to important parts and disregard unimportant parts. Though there are many variants and categories of attention mechanisms, each suited to different use cases and priorities, all attention mechanisms feature three core processes: A process of "reading" raw data sequences and converting them into vector embeddings, in which each element in the sequence is represented by its own feature vector(s). A process of accurately determining similarities, correlations and other dependencies (or lack thereof) between each vector, quantified as alignment scores (or attention scores) that reflect how aligned (or not aligned) they are. Alignment scores are then used to compute attention weights by using a softmax function, which normalizes all values to a range between 0-1 such that they all add up to a total of 1. So for instance, assigning an attention weight of 0 to an element means it should be ignored. An attention weight of 1 means that element should receive 100% attention because all other elements would have attention weights of 0 (because all weights must sum up to 1). In essence, the output of a softmax function is a probability distribution. A process of using those attention weights to emphasize or deemphasize the influence of specific input elements on how the model makes predictions. In other words, a means of using attention weights to help models focus on or ignore information. Queries, keys and values The seminal "Attention is All You Need" paper articulated its attention mechanism by using the terminology of a relational database: queries, keys and values. Relational databases are designed to simplify the storage and retrieval of relevant data: they assign a unique identifier ("key") to each piece of data, and each key is associated with a corresponding value. In NLP, a model's "database" is the vocabulary of tokens it has learned from its training dataset. The massive influence of the "Attention is All You Need" paper has resulted in even previous attention mechanisms often being retroactively described in these terms. Generally speaking, this conception of attention entails interaction between three types of vector representations for each token in a sequence. The query vector represents the information a given token is seeking. The key vectors represent the information that each token contains. Alignment between query and key is used to compute attention weights. The value (or value vector) applies the attention-weighted information from the key vectors. Contributions from keys that are strongly aligned with a query are weighted more heavily; contributions from keys that are not relevant to a query will be weighted closer to zero. Specific attention mechanism variants are differentiated primarily by how vectors are encoded, how alignment scores are calculated and attention weights are applied to provide the model with relevant information. Additive attention Badhanau's attention mechanism was designed specifically for machine translation. It uses a bidirectional RNN to encode each input token, processing the input sequence in both the forward direction and in reverse and concatenating the results together. This approach is particularly useful when, for example, the original and translated languages have different ordering conventions for nouns and adjectives. Here, the decoder hidden state at each timestep of the translated sentence is the equivalent of a query vector and the encoder hidden state at each step in the source sentence is the equivalent of a key vector. Alignment scores are then determined by a simple feedforward neural network, the attention layer, jointly trained with the rest of the model. This attention layer comprises up to three subsets of learnable model weights: query weights for the hidden decoder states ("Wq"), key weights for hidden encoder states ("Wk") and value weights to scale the final output ("wv"). These weights are the model's "knowledge": by adjusting the specific values of those weights during training to minimize a loss function, the model learns to make accurate translations. At each step, additive attention works as follows: The query vector (multiplied by Wq) is added to a key vector (multiplied by Wk). If they are aligned, adding them together will yield a large value. If they're irrelevant to one another, adding them together will yield a small value or negative value. The resulting number is input to a ? ? ? ? activation function, which maps all inputs to a number between -1 and 1. The output of the ? ? ? ? function is then multiplied by the value weights wv. This yields the alignment score between the query vector and that key vector. The alignment score is then input to a softmax function, which yields an attention weight for that key vector. The context vector that the decoder uses to generate the translated sentence is calculated as the attention-weighted sum of each key vector. One benefit of additive attention is that it does not require query and key vectors to be the same length. Dot product attention In 2015, Luong et al introduced several novel methodologies to simplify and enhance Badhanau's attention mechanism for machine translation. Perhaps their most notable contribution was a new alignment score function that used multiplication instead of addition. It also eschewed the ? ? ? ? function, calculating the similarity between hidden state vectors by using their dot product. Learn more: PMC Disclaimer | PMC Copyright Notice Sci Rep. 2025 Dec 17;16:2869. doi: 10.1038/s41598-025-32639-x Contextual priority attention enables linear time sequence modeling in transformers Karim Ben Khaled 1,2,?, Davy Monticolo 1,2 Author information Article notes Copyright and License information PMCID: PMC12828051 PMID: 41408385 Abstract The quadratic computational complexity of the self-attention mechanism in Transformer models severely constrains their applicability to long sequence inputs. We propose Contextual Priority Attention (CPA), a novel attention mechanism that reduces computational complexity from to theoretically, with experimentally observed linear scaling, while preserving the essential contextual modeling capabilities of traditional attention. Unlike existing efficient attention variants that approximate the full attention matrix, CPA fundamentally reimagines attention as a global-context-driven priority system. Our approach first computes a Global Context Vector (GCV) to capture the overall sequence information, then uses this context to assign priority scores to individual tokens, enabling sparse attention allocation. In encoder-decoder architectures, we apply CPA to the encoder while maintaining standard attention in the decoder, achieving substantial efficiency improvements while preserving full model expressivity for sequence-to-sequence tasks. Through theoretical analysis and extensive experimentation across language understanding, translation, and long document tasks, we demonstrate that CPA achieves comparable performance to standard self-attention while offering significant efficiency gains. On long-sequence benchmarks (8K+ tokens), CPA outperforms traditional Transformers and state-of-the-art efficient attention variants while using substantially fewer computational resources. Our findings suggest that pairwise token interactions may be unnecessary for effective contextual modeling, opening new avenues for efficient large-scale language models. Subject terms: Engineering, Mathematics and computing Introduction Transformer-based models1 have revolutionized natural language processing and many other domains of artificial intelligence. Their success stems largely from the self-attention mechanism, which enables each element in a sequence to attend to all other elements, capturing complex dependencies regardless of positional distance. However, this attention mechanism scales quadratically with sequence length, leading to significant computational and memory constraints when processing long inputs. This quadratic scaling poses a fundamental challenge for applications requiring long context, such as document-level machine translation, long-form question answering, and whole-document analysis. While various approaches have been proposed to address this bottleneck2-5, most attempt to approximate standard self-attention through techniques such as low-rank approximations, localized attention patterns, or kernel methods. In this paper, we introduce Contextual Priority Attention (CPA), which takes a fundamentally different approach. Rather than approximating the pairwise attention matrix, CPA reimagines attention as a global-to-local relevance filtering process inspired by cognitive theories of human attention6,7. Our approach first computes a Global Context Vector (GCV) that captures the "big picture" of the input sequence. Then, using this global context, we compute a priority score for each input element, measuring its relevance to the current context. Finally, we apply a sparse transformation to these scores, allowing the model to focus exclusively on the most relevant elements (see Fig. 1). Fig. 1. Open in a new tab Overview of the Contextual Priority Attention mechanism. (a) First, a Global Context Vector (GCV) is computed from the input sequence using a learned weighted average. (b) The GCV is concatenated with each token to compute token-specific priority scores via an MLP. (c) Sparse attention weights are generated by applying sparsemax to the priority scores. (d) The output is computed as a weighted sum of value projections, using only tokens with non-zero attention weights. CPA offers several key advantages: Linear computational complexity () with respect to sequence length Interpretable attention patterns with explicit token prioritization Adaptive sparsity that adjusts to input complexity Theoretical capacity to capture both local and global dependencies Through extensive experimentation on multiple tasks including machine translation, language modeling, and long document classification, we demonstrate that CPA achieves performance competitive with full attention while significantly reducing computational requirements, especially for long sequences. Our contributions are as follows: We propose Contextual Priority Attention, a novel attention mechanism with theoretical complexity that empirically demonstrates linear scaling, based on global-context-driven prioritization. We provide theoretical analysis showing that CPA can approximate full attention under certain conditions while maintaining linear complexity. We empirically demonstrate competitive performance with state-of-the-art models across multiple tasks. We analyze the emergent attention patterns, showing how CPA learns meaningful prioritization strategies. Related work Efficient attention mechanisms The quadratic complexity of self-attention has inspired numerous approaches to improve efficiency. These can be broadly categorized into several strategies: Pattern-based sparsity: Methods like Sparse Transformer2 and Longformer8 limit attention to predefined patterns, such as local windows, dilated windows, or fixed global tokens. BlockBERT9 and BigBird10 use block-sparse attention patterns. While effective, these approaches incorporate structural biases that may not align with the actual dependencies in the data. Learnable sparsity: Methods such as Reformer3 use locality-sensitive hashing to dynamically identify similar tokens that should attend to each other. Routing Transformer11 employs content-based clustering. These approaches reduce complexity but still fundamentally rely on pairwise token interactions. Low-rank approximations: Linformer4 projects the key and value matrices to lower dimensions, achieving linear complexity. However, this approach struggles with variable-length inputs and loses the flexibility of the original attention mechanism. Kernel methods: Performers5 and Linear Transformers12 rewrite the softmax attention using kernel methods, approximating the attention matrix implicitly. While mathematically elegant, these methods may sacrifice some of the expressivity of the original attention mechanism. Recurrence-based methods: Models like Transformer-XL13 and Compressive Transformer14 incorporate recurrence to handle long sequences. These approaches maintain the standard attention within segments but use recurrent connections between segments. Table 1 provides a comparative analysis of these approaches. Our Contextual Priority Attention differs fundamentally from these approaches by eliminating pairwise comparisons entirely, instead using global context to guide token-specific attention allocation. Table 1. Comparison of efficient attention approaches. Approach Complexity Preserves full expressivity Handles variable length inputs Learnable patterns Implementation complexity Standard attention Low Pattern-based Sparsity Medium Learnable Sparsity Partial High Low-Rank Approximations Partial Medium Kernel Methods Partial Partial Medium Recurrence-based + Memory Partial High CPA (Ours) Theoretical Medium Open in a new tab Cognitive models of attention Our approach is loosely inspired by cognitive theories of human attention, which suggest that perception involves both bottom-up feature processing and top-down attentional control guided by current goals and context15,16. Particularly relevant is Broadbent's filter theory7, which proposes that cognitive processing employs selective filters to focus only on relevant stimuli. In neuroscience, the interaction between global brain states and local neural activity parallels our approach of using global context to guide local attention allocation17. Several computational models of attention in computer vision have implemented related concepts, particularly through top-down modulation of bottom-up saliency18,19. Sparse neural networks Our work also relates to research on sparse neural networks, particularly approaches that dynamically determine sparsity patterns. Techniques such as Sparse Mixture of Experts20,21 and conditional computation22,23 activate only relevant parts of the network based on input. These approaches demonstrate that sparse activation can achieve strong performance while improving computational efficiency. Contextual priority attention In this section, we describe our proposed Contextual Priority Attention mechanism in detail, first presenting the intuition and then formalizing the approach. Intuition Traditional self-attention computes pairwise interactions between all tokens in a sequence, requiring comparisons for a sequence of length n. This exhaustive approach implicitly assumes that every token-to-token relationship is potentially informative and must be explicitly evaluated. However, this assumption may be unnecessarily conservative for many natural language tasks, where the semantic content of a sequence can often be summarized more compactly. Human attention operates fundamentally differently. Cognitive research suggests that we do not exhaustively compare every perceived element to every other element. Instead, we rapidly construct a holistic understanding of our environment-a "gist" or mental model-and then selectively attend to elements that are most relevant to our current goals and context16,24. This two-stage process of global comprehension followed by selective focus allows humans to efficiently process complex scenes without cognitive overload. CPA draws direct inspiration from this cognitive model. Rather than asking "how relevant is token A to token B?" for all possible pairs, we decompose attention into two sequential stages: Global comprehension: First, we compute a Global Context Vector (GCV) that captures a compressed, holistic representation of the entire input sequence. This vector serves as a summary of "what is this sequence about?" Selective prioritization: Then, for each token, we evaluate a single question: "how relevant is this token to the global context?" This yields a priority score indicating contextual importance. This reformulation reduces the computational burden from pairwise comparisons to n context-relative evaluations, while preserving the essential selective nature of attention. Figure 2 illustrates this fundamental conceptual difference between standard self-attention and CPA. Fig. 2. Open in a new tab Conceptual comparison between standard self-attention (left) and Contextual Priority Attention (right). Standard attention computes all pairwise interactions between tokens, resulting in quadratic complexity. CPA first computes a global context representation, then evaluates each token against this shared context, achieving linear complexity. To illustrate with a concrete example, consider processing the sentence: "The cat, which had been sleeping peacefully on the warm windowsill all afternoon, suddenly jumped down." Standard self-attention would compute interactions, including many between tokens with minimal semantic relationship (e.g., "peacefully" and "down"). In contrast, CPA first forms a global understanding that this sentence describes a cat's action, then prioritizes tokens most relevant to this context-likely "cat," "sleeping," and "jumped"-while assigning lower priority to modifiers and function words. This approach offers an additional benefit beyond computational efficiency: it provides an implicit regularization effect. By forcing the model to route all attention decisions through a shared global context, CPA encourages the learning of representations that capture semantically meaningful aspects of the input rather than spurious local correlations. The global context acts as an information bottleneck25, filtering out noise while retaining task-relevant signal. By computing relevance scores against a shared global context, we can prioritize tokens holistically, focusing computational resources on the most contextually important elements while naturally filtering out irrelevant ones. This design philosophy "global understanding before local selection" mirrors not only human cognition but also efficient algorithms in other domains, such as hierarchical search and coarse-to-fine processing in computer vision26. In our experiments, the learned average approach offered the best balance of performance and efficiency. The priority scoring function effectively measures how relevant each token is to the current global context, without requiring pairwise comparisons between tokens.
